item.title: Other Possible Edits
item.content:encoded:
+ show block
– hide block

I made two edits to the article that I knew were unintentional typos (details in history), but I wanted to bring to the attention of the author a few aspects of the article that I don't feel comfortable changing on my own.

  • Reference to "Item-001" vacillates between using "is"/"are" throughout the article, when only one should probably be used.
  • "materials necessary to construct a necessary"
    • Possible opportunity for change of duplicate word usage.
  • There isn't consistency in spacing after/between numbers and their units (e.g. 20m, 10 km, 5km, etc).
  • "and cannot express to how important this is"
    • Needs the addition of a "you" or the removal of "to".
  • "That's why the Fritzwilliams"
    • It appears as though "the Administrator" was being thought of when "Fritzwilliams" was typed.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
All SCP-001 proposals must answer questions. Usually, that question is, "where did the Foundation come from?" Some answer questions about the nature of SCP-001 (such as Kate's proposal). This one, however, answers a question I didn't even know I asked: "what would happen if the Foundation could neutralize anomalies?"

And, as the old saying goes, absolute power corrupts absolutely.

The best part about this is that the SCP itself actually works, with no drawbacks. More than anything else, this SCP is a commentary on human nature, and our inherent failings. A perfect device, a literal deus ex machina, wasted because of the greed and ambition of one man.

But people don't learn, do they? O5-13 certainly didn't.

I disliked SCP-2000 because it felt cheap - it was a device that could reset reality at will, which lowered the stakes to the point where it felt like nothing was scary. But the reason I enjoyed this so much was because it gives the Foundation a way to make the world safe, and inverts the trope in true tragic fashion.

I see what you did there. God, I see what you did there.

Well done, djkaktus. Thank you for making me think about the Foundationverse differently.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
So first, let's get into the guts of this thing:

+ line-by-line
- hide text

Containment Class: Keter-Thaumiel

I'm not a person who usually cares much about containment class arguments. Most of the time it's next to meaningless for me. And in this case it doesn't affect my vote. But I have to wonder, why do a split classification here? I'm not sure what's to be gained.

Containment Status: Active-Stable

And the same with this. Are these attempts at sowing new paradigms for future articles? Because I feel like I've been seeing a lot of this lately, with all the business about humes and whatnot. A little extraneous continuity here and there is fine, but it feels like we're getting a little overboard with it.

Automated, closed-circuit surveillance drones are to maintain the perimeter around Item-001's containment site, and have been designed to kill on-sight.

Technologically advanced murder drones that immediately kill trespassers at the edge of a 10 km security cordon in Mexico somewhere. Seems to me that might raise more than a few questions.

The containment of information regarding SCP-001, formerly Item-001

But…it says Item-001 in the current version of the document.

often in excess of ███GJ,

I'm unsure why that needs to be censored. If anything, knowing the actual amount might lend more otherworldliness to the anomaly.

1485992-Thirteen Men On A Dead Man's Ship-4910581

I realize that "code phrases what be all mysterious like" is a well-worn device around here, but I always find it to be kind of goofy when I encounter it, and it's no different here. The sheer number of times it happens in this document kind of heightens my tiredness of this conceit.

Under guise of a nuclear-testing facility for the United States government, a site will be constructed in Northern Mexico, away from civilian populations, in order to safely test these theories.

So, about this point. Your project begins in 1922, but the US government would not have had any "nuclear testing facilities" in the 1920s. Any nuclear power-related research couldn't have really begun in earnest until the early 1930s, and research into nuclear armaments didn't begin in the US until 1939. This is far enough out for this to feel immediately anachronistic to anyone familiar with the subject material.

Also, why in the world would the Foundation pick post-revolutionary Mexico as a testing site for this project? Under American auspices, no less? Given the recent instability in that very area, anti-US sentiment that is certain to be present in the area (the Pancho Villa Expedition is going to be pretty fresh in peoples' memories), this seems like a poor choice for somewhere where you want to be doing things unobserved. Especially for a project like this.

An attack on a Foundation research facility in the Sudan by Kingdom of Abaddon forces increased the drastic need for a long-range defense system

Somewhat minor nitpick here, but "increased the drastic need" feels a little odd. "Drastic" usually is applied to actions, not states of being. A better way to phrase might be "underscored the need" or "increased the urgency in developing" or something.

The town of San March then became the new Testing Site 001

I'm assuming you mean San Marco here.

do not tread heavily through the lives of these innocents. God knows enough blood has been shed on our behalf, I do not wish to spill more.

This treads kind of close to narm territory. I get that it's a 001 Proposal and more dramatic language is usually warranted, but maybe consider dialing back this part just a bit.

Class I Reality Bending entities

I've said it before in other peoples' articles, and I'll say it again here. There's got to be a better term than "Reality Bending" to be used for stuff like this.

However, due to inbreeding and other genetic malfunctions that plague their society, GOI-003 is particularly fragile and will likely not last on its own as an independent organization for any longer than 20 years.

So, I'm not a geneticist nor a doctor, but this struck me as odd. How long has this society existed that inbreeding is a problem? And if it's such a problem that this group's society is going to collapse in 20 years, how do they manage to serve as an existential threat?

Now, I like to see ambition in 001 proposals, and this certainly has that. I also like a complex-yet-coherent narrative, and despite some of the stuff pointed out above, this is that too. The weapon at the center of this is horrific enough to engender interest, and I salute the attempt to provide an actual reason for the existence of the Chaos Insurgency, even if I wish they were nowhere on the wiki in any form (and thanks for avoiding that hideous name, by the way).

What primarily kept this from working for me on a conceptual level, however, was that as I read this the first time, from the very beginning "what could possibly go right?" was all that ran through my head. And sure enough, things go horribly wrong. Some logic can occasionally be sacrificed for the purpose of a good story, but it just seemed way too ridiculous that there would a system of five failsafes or whatever for the 001 entity itself in case it went rogue, but turning the whole thing over to a single operator with no checks on him whatosever? Sure, why not, it's not like having absolute power to destroy anything on Earth is going to have any effect on anyone, right? The idea that the Foundation would just turn over the reins to something like this to a single guy with absolutely no plan to keep him under control is completely ludicrous.

Because of that issue, I could see the arc of the narrative coming from the very beginning, and things kind of played out in exactly the way that I expected them to. Coupled with what seemed to me to be a giant lapse in common sense being sort of handwaved away, the whole thing felt like a giant contrivance, and I just could not get into this article.

Also, about the footnotes. I'm concerned that this article is going to be further encouragement for people to shovel these things in because it's the Thing to Do Now, which to me is a problem because what it is at heart is handwaving away things with Official-Sounding Words. It was a neat trick the first couple of times, I suppose, but the way these are employed, there's really no reason to not append a footnote every time some sort of pronouncement on the anomalous is made, which makes this whole device lack coherency to me. I appreciate you not going apeshit with it, but it's filler waiting to happen, really. And as a final note, the vigorousness of the peer review process for publishing scientific works would lead me to doubt that the Foundation would go so far as to publish multiple scholarly journals with which to make these notations.

It's not a bad article. There are parts that are enjoyable, and lapses notwithstanding, it's written to a stylistic level that I expect from a talented writer. But when you up the ante by slapping the 001 label on a work and put together a correspondingly complex and long buildup, the execution needs to be fundamentally solid and the payoff needs to be worth it. Ultimately, the underlying issues in the narrative just affect too much about this for me to support this one.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I sincerely doubt they could survive in whatever realm they were sent to. They're reality benders, yes, but the transport is instantaneous. They wouldn't be able to prepare themselves for whatever fresh hell they'd find themselves in. And even if they did, there are obviously some…things…very, very interested in humans(or else we wouldn't of been able to get their attention long enough to trap them in corpses).

I mean, you saw the bit where it said they went through a ludicrous amount of D-Class, right? I'm pretty sure that was us baiting them, as well as allowing us to study them for however long they were able to stay in our dimension. I believe that the reason we basically fried the children's neurons and other higher-functioning portions of the brain was twofold;

One, it *seems* like they can inhabit a body just fine, it's the brain trying to transmit the eldritch-thing's "thoughts" that causes the bodies to break down. Like plugging a hairdryer into a nuclear power-plant and giving it all the juice. No neural receptors and such, no transmission of thoughts, no overloading the body.

Two, there was a very real possibility they might've been able to learn how to use a functioning human brain and the like without the body self-destructing, and thus be able to exert their power in our world of their own volition. By removing that from the equation, we've made it impossible for them to leave and impossible for them to act without a very specific series of words and/or actions(the Trigger).

Oh, and as a bonus, here's something else that dawned on me:

We've got a Schrodinger's Cat here. We can't observe them, they cannot observe one another or themselves. We have them in a state between life & death, existence & non-existence.

Or, in short: That which is not dead can eternal lie..

item.content:encoded:
I'm upvoting this, but I want to make sure I've wrapped my head around it.

Basically, the Foundation figured out(roughly) how reality benders worked. Quantum entanglement allowing for the manipulation of particles at any distance so long as you're aware of what it is, because when you gain knowledge of an object you're changing it. So, with that noted, they use quantum tunneling to more or less say "fuck you" to the very concept of three-dimensional space and circumvent the problem with a different dimension(like making two points on a piece of paper, folding it and pushing the pencil through is the actual shortest route between them).

So, using this dimension, they take energy from it and use it to shunt the target into that dimension(so that they aren't breaking the whole "energy cannot be created or destroyed" rule). The target isn't being annihilated it's being *moved* to someplace outside of (our) three-dimensional space.

And apparently we accomplished this by finding something that 'lived' in those dimensions and used what amounts to scientific necromancy to entice them into bodies we'd fried so that they couldn't actually *use* them. We've stuffed eldritch gods into child's corpses, that which are not dead but can eternal lie. So they're stuck, and can only "react" when given outside stimulation. That's the Trigger. That's why they haven't eaten us. They can't.

This is awesome. Fuck you, Hitler, the holocaust was quaint but the Foundation just weaponized *despair*.

*mic drop*

item.content:encoded:
I like the subtle format shift for the early 20th century Foundation. That said, this feels like it's trying to do too much with too little. This death ray powered by forsaken children and the story surrounding it is responsible (completely or in part) for the formation of the O5 Council, the Thaumiel classification, a great deal of the in-universe reasoning behind forbidding crosstests, among other things

I still upvoted, because it was brilliant technically, and very well-written, but it just seems a bit underwhelming when you look at it as a whole.

Now, for a nit that is too big not to be picked
Nuclear power in the 1920's?

This document states that the site for containing the Item is disguised as a nuclear testing facility, and makes extensive reference to radiation poisoning, in the 1920's. While radioactivity was well known by then, and there had been talk of harnessing energy from radioactive elements, actual nuclear fission wasn't discovered until the 1930's. Radiation poisoning was not seriously studied until the mid-1940's. I suppose it's plausible that the Foundation could have discovered both early, being on the cutting edge as they are often depicted, but, at the very least, they would not use a government nuclear testing facility as a cover story.
